newsitem.title: USA: Iranian envoy urges U.N. conference on Afghanistan.
newsitem.headline: Iranian envoy urges U.N. conference on Afghanistan.

text.p: Iran's U.N. ambassador called in a Washington Post article Monday for a U.N.-sponsored conference on the conflict in Afghanistan and accused the United States of sabotaging Tehran's mediation efforts.
"Iran supports the U.N. initiative to convene an international meeting of states concerned with Afghanistan in the near future as a first step," envoy Kamal Kharrazi said.

Despite the purist Islamic creed of Afghanistan's Taleban movement, which captured Kabul in September, its successes have alarmed Tehran which continues to support the ousted government of President Burhanuddin Rabbani.

Kharrazi said Afghans needed urgent international help to overcome the cycle of violence in their country, and said efforts by interested states, the U.N. and the Organisation of Islamic Conference were the "only viable approach".

The Iranian envoy attacked U.S. policies in Afghanistan and other states in the region, saying "Iran's efforts at conciliation for political settlement of disputes invariably have faced overt and covert U.S. sabotage".

Washington's real motive, he said, was to enforce a semblance of security in Afghanistan so that a proposed oil and gas pipeline from Central Asia to the Indian Ocean could go through Afghanistan and not through Iran.

Kharrazi's article, published on the 17th anniversary of the takeover of the U.S. embassy in Iran by Moslem militants, followed a conference in Tehran last week which called for an end to fighting in Afghanistan and for U.N.-backed peace talks.

The United States initially showed interest in starting a dialogue with Taleban, but later backed off when the movement failed to gain control of the whole country and drew hostile U.S. media coverage with Islamic restrictions on women.
Washington has said it supports efforts by U.N. envoy Norbert Holl to broker a ceasefire and start peace talks.
Despite Kharrazi's anti-U.S. rhetoric, the Washington Post said in an editorial that his article in fact "seeks to engage the United States in a negotiation over Afghanistan".

It said that despite hostility between the two countries, U.S. planners remained interested in a dialogue with Iran. The problem was that Iran refused to address U.S. concerns over alleged Iranian backing for terrorism and other issues, it said.
